hlni.insight: The same total credit count can be composed of entirely different academic modules.
hlni.audienceGap: Students assume that if two degrees share similar credit totals, they are interchangeable or equal in focus.
hlni.viewerChange: The viewer stops equating 'total credits' with 'identical experience' and learns to request a module breakdown.
hlni.support: The comparison follows a logical breakdown of components versus aggregates, proving that the sum does not define the composition.
hlni.payoff: The viewer now has a practical method: ignore the total and request the module list to make a decision.

reelTitle: B.Com vs BBA: The Total Value Mystery
objective: Teach students to look beyond aggregate labels
targetAudience: A broad +2 student audience discovering ideas, courses, or student experiences

shots.name: The Hook
shots.visual: Split screen. Left side: 'B.Com (100 Credits)'. Right side: 'BBA (100 Credits)'. Both totals blink.
shots.dialogue: Think B.Com and BBA are the same because the credit totals match?

shots.name: The Reveal
shots.visual: The numbers slide and expand into lists. B.Com shows deep accounting/tax modules. BBA shows case study/strategy modules.
shots.dialogue: Look closer. The aggregate is identical, but the internal components—the actual tasks—are built for different goals.

shots.name: The Payoff
shots.visual: Hand removes the total label. Student points to specific module names.
shots.dialogue: Don't judge by the total. Ask for the module breakdown. Compare the actual tasks, not the labels.

productionNotes.editing: Snappy rhythm matched to graphic transitions

creativeSummary.keyCreativeIdea: Use a mathematical visual to show that identical credit totals can mask different academic content.

selected.title: The Total Value Mystery
selected.audienceGap: Assuming that degrees with similar total credit counts are functionally identical.
selected.hlni: The same total can result from different component values; an aggregate alone cannot tell you the underlying mix.
selected.viewerChange: Understands that the same total can be composed of very different academic experiences.
selected.concept: Visualizing two identical numerical totals that, when expanded, reveal completely different course compositions.
selected.device: A sliding scale animation showing how 100 credits can be divided differently, challenging the viewer to ask for the breakdown.
selected.support: The claim follows from the displayed arithmetic, not an invented university metric.
methodSteps: Show two clearly illustrative component lists with the same total.
Ask for the breakdown before drawing a conclusion from the total.
selected.interpretationRule: Use the breakdown to ask what differs; do not infer identical experiences from equal totals.
selected.visibleProof: An explicitly illustrative arithmetic counterexample makes the hidden difference visible.
selected.payoff: Use the breakdown to ask what differs; do not infer identical experiences from equal totals.
selected.limitations: Keep figures clearly illustrative and do not assign them to actual programmes, credits or outcomes.

comparedWith.hlni: A task label alone does not tell you what you must produce, what will be assessed, or what feedback you receive. Ask these as separate questions.
comparedWith.device: Direct address to camera using the worksheet to show that 'Marketing' or 'Accounting' tasks can have vastly different assessment criteria.

comparedWith.hlni: A short illustrative activity can reveal where you need help or what you want to investigate next; it cannot determine which degree suits you.
comparedWith.device: Natural conversation showing that being 'stuck' on a specific detail is a productive starting point for a better question.

comparedWith.hlni: The same total can result from different component values; an aggregate alone cannot tell you the underlying mix.
comparedWith.device: A sliding scale animation showing how 100 credits can be divided differently, challenging the viewer to ask for the breakdown.

conceptSelection.contrast: Trust uses a structural auditing tool to build credibility; Connection uses a personal journaling process to normalize inquiry; Discovery uses a mathematical counterexample to challenge assumptions about degree equivalence.
